A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Added material and relocated sections can be distinguished reliably.

before.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix B.2 report original numerical gradient/Hessian comparisons on a synthetic simplex function, including fitted dimension-dependent slope ratios.

after.justification: Appendix B.3 retains this original numerical study, including the scatter plots and fitted slope-ratio curve in Figures 1–2.

M1.justification: All five optimization procedures are retained. Replacing η_t with η in the mirror-descent update makes explicit the constant step size already required by v1's Theorem 1.

E1.justification: Both versions numerically evaluate the same synthetic function on simplices of varying dimension. The newly added exponential and logistic examples are mathematical analyses, not additional evaluated datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The numerical comparison still contrasts Euclidean and primal-dual smoothness characterizations. New Appendix A discusses relative smoothness without adding an experimentally evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: V1 Appendix B.2 and v2 Appendix B.3 retain 500 sampled simplex points, the same norm measurements, and the slope-ratio sweep from dimension 6 to 198 in increments of 3.

E4.justification: The existing dimension-sensitivity analysis is retained. No ablations, robustness tests or empirical case studies are added; the new Appendix B.1 examples are theoretical derivations.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the numerical study. New random-sphere expectation bounds are theoretical results, not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The matched plots retain the same observations and fitted curve, 1.87 n^-0.43, with the same reported O(n^-0.4) trend. Table 1's five convergence rates also remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds Proposition 2 and Appendix B.1 derivations for exponential and logistic objectives, dimension-dependent link-function ratios, random-sphere expectation bounds and bounded-domain cases. Appendix A adds mathematical comparison arguments. The original quadratic proposition survives as Proposition 3, and the main convergence theorems and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: arbitrary-norm generalized smoothness, the self-bounding property, classical convergence rates for mirror-type algorithms, and anytime stochastic convergence under generalized bounded noise.

C2.justification: V2 explains the examples' relevance on bounded domains, adds practical objections to relative smoothness in Appendix A, and states in Remark 5 that the stochastic bound's extra logarithmic factors are unimprovable.

D1.justification: The PyTorch-autograd calculations, linear-programming description, sampling instructions and dimension grid are retained. No new implementation instructions, hardware details or code/data access information are supplied.

R1.justification: The brief relative-smoothness discussion becomes a dedicated critical comparison in Appendix A, substantially expanding positioning against an alternative framework. V2 also adds reinforcement-learning and LLM-alignment literature and substantively revises its account of Tyurin's results.

P1.justification: Section 3.2 is rewritten around the new examples, the earlier examples remain in Appendix B, and the properties appendix moves from A to C. The remaining narrative and proofs largely retain their wording and organization, with local language and notation edits.

P2.justification: The slope plot moves from v1's main-text Figure 1 to v2's appendix Figure 2; the appendix scatter plot becomes Figure 1. Captions and surrounding layout change, while both plots and Table 1 retain their displays.

improvement.justification: The added logistic examples and bounded-domain discussion improve motivation, but new Appendix A introduces a faulty comparison argument: its assertion that g(x)=exp(||x||_2^2/2) is (0,||x||_2+1)-smooth violates the stated inequality for 0<||x||_2<1. These explanatory gains coexist with reduced mathematical reliability in the new material, while the core results remain unchanged, leaving the net quality effect unclear.
